analysis.one_liner: Repeals the minimum tax that keeps large corporations from using deductions and credits to escape paying tax.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the corporate minimum tax was never acted on: it drew no cosponsors and died in the Senate Finance Committee at the end of 2000.
analysis.plain_summary: Corporations normally pay a 35% tax on profits, but deductions and credits can reduce that to zero. The corporate alternative minimum tax is a parallel calculation that sets a floor: a large corporation must pay at least a minimum amount no matter how many write-offs it claims. This bill would have repealed that floor entirely [S2][S3]. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on January 19, 1999 and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Large profitable corporations that currently owe the minimum tax would have gained, because they could again use depreciation write-offs, credits, and other deductions to reduce their federal tax to zero. The companies most affected are capital-intensive businesses with large write-offs, such as manufacturers and energy companies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large profitable corporations with big write-offs

how_it_helps.text: The bill terminates the corporate alternative minimum tax for all taxable years beginning after enactment [S3].
The corporate minimum tax exists so that corporations with substantial deductions and credits still pay a baseline amount of federal tax [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would have lost the revenue the minimum tax collects from large corporations, and the cost would fall on everyone else through higher deficits or through other taxes making up the difference.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the minimum tax would have removed the guarantee that highly profitable corporations pay at least some federal income tax, cutting federal revenue at the time of the bill [S2][S3].

Supporters of the corporate minimum tax argue it prevents companies with billions in profits from paying nothing while other businesses and individual taxpayers shoulder the load; repeal would end that check without any replacement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's entire substance was one thing: ending the corporate minimum tax [S2][S3]. Despite its name, it contained no provisions offsetting the lost revenue or addressing any other corporate tax issue. The benefit would have flowed to a narrow set of large corporations with enough write-offs to trigger the minimum tax, while the cost was spread across every federal taxpayer.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, sat there for two years with no hearing, no markup, and no cosponsors, and expired when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Kyl of Arizona introduced the Corporate Tax Equity Act on January 19, 1999 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action was taken after the committee referral; the bill received no hearing or vote and died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, nothing changed: the corporate minimum tax remained on the books, and the federal government kept collecting it from large corporations. No industry gained; the outcome simply preserved the existing tax floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; corporate minimum tax stayed in place

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 19, 1999 and delivered introductory remarks; no colleague joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors or recorded opponents emerged, so the partisan shape of any potential floor fight is unknown.

industries.industry: Large capital-intensive corporations (manufacturers, energy and other companies with large depreciation write-offs)
industries.note: These are the companies most likely to owe the corporate minimum tax, because their deductions and credits reduce their regular tax; the bill would have freed them from it, but it died. Their interest ran against the public's, since repeal would have cost the Treasury revenue that other taxpayers ultimately fund.
